Inflammatory Disorders of the CNS

UNE COM · Neurology · Disease Index

🧠 Multiple Sclerosis

LO 1–5 F:M ≈ 2–3:1 Onset 20–40y CNS demyelination
An inflammatory demyelinating disorder of heterogeneous origin — the most common cause of neurologic disability in young adults after trauma, driven by a classic triad of inflammation, demyelination, and gliosis.
At-a-glance overview — epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnostics, symptom map, and management
▶
▶ Multiple sclerosis — causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology
Video — "Multiple sclerosis - causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology" (YouTube)
1 Natural History

Epidemiology & Genetics

  • Second only to trauma as a cause of neurologic disability in young adults; incidence 0.3–0.8/1,000; US prevalence ~1/1,000 (~10,000 new cases/yr); >2 million affected worldwide
  • Temperate climates, higher socioeconomic groups, ↑ prevalence farther from the equator
  • Onset typically 20–40y; F:M ≈ 2–3:1
  • Genetic predisposition: HLA-DRB1*15 ↑ risk, HLA-A*02 protective; 35% concordance in monozygotic twins vs. 3–4% in first-degree relatives
  • Environmental risk factors: low vitamin D, cigarette smoking, EBV/HHV-6 exposure, early-life obesity

Pathophysiology

Autoimmune inflammation is the central pathogenic process. Autoreactive T-cells activate → perivenular lymphocytic cuffing (inflammatory cells collar the venules) → focal demyelination with partial axon preservation (acute plaque) → progressive axonal loss and oligodendrocyte atrophy (chronic plaque) → gliosis → inadequate remyelination.

B-cell involvement is increasingly recognized: anti-CD20 agents (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, rituximab) prevent exacerbations, oligoclonal IgG bands are found intrathecally, and tertiary lymphoid organs appear in the meninges in secondary progressive MS. Progressive phenotypes show chronic compartmentalized inflammation behind an intact blood-brain barrier with accelerated brain atrophy.

Autoreactive T-cell activation
→
Perivenular lymphocytic cuffing
→
Focal demyelination (acute plaque)
→
Axonal loss + oligodendrocyte atrophy (chronic plaque)
→
Gliosis
→
Inadequate remyelination
Four Clinical Courses
Clinical courses of MS — disability trajectory over time by phenotype
Relapsing-Remitting (RRMS)

~85–90% of cases. Exacerbations with full or partial recovery between attacks — the most common course at onset.

Secondary Progressive (SPMS)

>50% of RRMS patients eventually convert: continuous worsening independent of relapses, ± further superimposed attacks.

Primary Progressive (PPMS)

~10–15% of cases; M = F (unlike the female-predominant RRMS). Continuous worsening from onset, occasionally with plateaus.

Progressive-Relapsing (PRMS)

<5% of cases. Progressively worsening course from the start, but with superimposed attacks along the way.

Prognosis Pearl

Poor prognostic factors: male sex, onset age >40, multiple symptoms with early motor/cerebellar involvement, incomplete recovery after exacerbations, and a high relapse rate in the first 2 years.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation

Most Typical Presentations

  • Optic neuritis — often the first sign; unilateral, painful with eye movement, ↓color vision, RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil); fundoscopy is normal in ~60% (retrobulbar inflammation)
  • Sensory loss / paresthesias — patchy, may include a sensory ataxia
  • Weakness — pyramidal tract signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski, impaired gait
  • Oculomotor dysfunction — diplopia; internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO, more often bilateral) from an MLF plaque in the pons/midbrain: ipsilateral medial rectus weakness with contralateral abducting nystagmus, convergence intact
Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia

MLF lesion → impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye + nystagmus of the abducting contralateral eye on lateral gaze. Convergence spared.

Transverse Myelitis

Partial (asymmetric) cord transection from a demyelinating plaque — a common early MS manifestation causing asymmetric deficits below the lesion.

Cerebellar Signs

Ataxic gait, Charcot triad — scanning speech, nystagmus, intention tremor.

Other Findings

Bladder/bowel disturbance, mild cognitive deficits and depression, frontal lobe signs, absent abdominal reflexes, downward pronator drift (vs. cerebellar lesions which cause upward pronation/drift), neuropathic pain. Lhermitte's sign — electric shock sensation down the spine with neck flexion. Uhthoff phenomenon — reversible symptom worsening with ↑body temperature (heat, exercise, fever); resolves on cooling and is not a true relapse.

Red Flag

Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient should raise concern for MS — TN typically manifests unilaterally, so bilaterality is atypical enough to prompt an MS workup.

3 Diagnostic Workup

McDonald Criteria

Diagnosis requires demonstrating dissemination in space (DIS) — lesions in more than one typical CNS location — and dissemination in time (DIT) — new lesions appearing over time — confirmed clinically, on MRI, or via CSF. A single MRI showing both an enhancing (active) and non-enhancing (older) lesion can satisfy DIT without waiting for a second clinical attack.

History / PE FindingLabs / Imaging to Confirm
Optic neuritis, INO, sensory level, Lhermitte sign, downward pronator drift, cerebellar signsMRI brain + spine (study of choice) — periventricular plaques with Dawson fingers (radial extensions along medullary veins), infratentorial & spinal cord lesions, ± contrast enhancement (active lesion, typically resolves 2–8 weeks)
Suspected demyelinating disease, atypical presentationLP / CSF — oligoclonal IgG bands present in CSF but absent in serum (highly suggestive), moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis, ↑ myelin basic protein
Rule out mimics before committing to the diagnosisCBC, vitamin B12, TSH, ESR, ANA, RPR, Lyme serology, HIV, antiphospholipid/anti-SSA/anti-SSB antibodies
Subclinical lesion suspected but not seen on MRIEvoked potentials (visual, somatosensory) — reveal delayed conduction from clinically silent plaques
MRI (T2, axial) — solitary hyperintense demyelinated plaque in the telencephalon; multiple periventricular & mesencephalic hyperintensities
MRI (FLAIR, axial) — Dawson fingers: linear/ovoid periventricular hyperintensity perpendicular to the lateral ventricle, from perivascular inflammation around subependymal veins
Baseline images (1/2) — extensive bilateral periventricular demyelinating plaques with radial Dawson-finger extensions
Disease progression (2/2) — confluent periventricular hyperintensities with generalized cerebral atrophy, progressed from baseline
Cranial MRI (T2, axial) — T2 hyperintensity in the left middle cerebellar peduncle, periventricular to the fourth ventricle: a typical infratentorial demyelination site
Cervical spine MRI (T2, sagittal) — poorly defined hyperintensity at C4 within the cord; MS spinal plaques are usually shorter than two vertebral bodies
Periventricular signal abnormality — further periventricular white matter hyperintensity supporting dissemination in space
4 Treatment

Acute Exacerbation

First line: high-dose IV or PO glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone, prednisone) to shorten the attack. Alternatives: plasmapheresis or ACTH gel if refractory to steroids.

Disease-Modifying Therapy (long-term)
Interferon Beta / Glatiramer Acetate

Interferon beta suppresses T-cell activity and CNS lymphocyte invasion (SE: flu-like symptoms, injection reactions, liver dysfunction, depression). Glatiramer acetate acts as a myelin decoy, shifting Th1→Th2 (SE: injection/postinjection reactions, lipoatrophy).

Monoclonal Antibodies

Natalizumab (anti-α4-integrin, blocks CNS lymphocyte entry) and ocrelizumab/ofatumumab (anti-CD20, deplete B-cells) are highest-efficacy but carry PML risk.

Fumarates / Teriflunomide

Dimethyl fumarate (immunomodulator, anti-inflammatory) and teriflunomide (inhibits pyrimidine synthesis) — both used for relapsing MS and clinically isolated syndrome.

S1P Modulators

Fingolimod, siponimod — sequester lymphocytes in lymph nodes, reducing CNS invasion (SE: bradycardia, macular edema, infection risk).

Symptom-Targeted Therapy
Spasticity

Baclofen (GABA agonist), tizanidine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin.

Neuropathic Pain

TCAs (amitriptyline), duloxetine, carbamazepine, gabapentin.

Bladder / Gait

Oxybutynin/tolterodine for urgency; dalfampridine for walking speed.

5 Monitoring & Complications

Monitoring

  • Track relapse frequency/severity and disability progression (EDSS)
  • Surveillance MRI for new/enlarging lesions — evidence of subclinical activity even between clinical relapses
  • Periodic labs while on disease-modifying therapy (LFTs, CBC, agent-specific monitoring)
  • Screen for depression at follow-up visits

Major Complications

Partial visual loss, bladder dysfunction, spasticity with impaired mobility, cognitive/mental deterioration, and (rarely) trigeminal neuralgia. Natalizumab and anti-CD20 agents carry a risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).

Special Population — Pregnancy

Exacerbation risk ↓ during pregnancy but ↑ in the postpartum period; the long-term disease course is unchanged overall. Disease-modifying therapy is generally avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Clinical Vignette
📋 Board-Style Vignette
A 29-year-old woman presents with two days of blurred vision and pain with movement in her right eye. She also mentions that six months ago she had several weeks of tingling in her left hand that resolved on its own. On exam, color vision is diminished in the right eye and a relative afferent pupillary defect is present. MRI of the brain shows several periventricular white matter lesions, some enhancing and some not, with a linear "Dawson finger" pattern.
What the vignette is testing: optic neuritis (painful, unilateral, ↓color vision, RAPD) plus a prior sensory episode — two attacks separated in time — with an MRI showing both an enhancing (new) and non-enhancing (old) lesion, satisfying dissemination in time on a single scan. This is the McDonald-criteria "gimme" stem for MS.

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

  • "eye pain that worsens with eye movement" + "decreased color vision" → optic neuritis
  • "one eye won't adduct on lateral gaze, other eye has nystagmus" → internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion)
  • "symptoms worsen in a hot shower / after exercise, then resolve" → Uhthoff phenomenon, not a true relapse
  • "electric shock sensation down the spine with neck flexion" → Lhermitte's sign
  • "young woman, several neurologic complaints months apart, temperate climate" → framing for dissemination in space + time
  • "bands present in the CSF but not in the serum" → oligoclonal IgG bands, an MS-specific buzz phrase
  • "bilateral trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient" → atypical presentation that should trigger an MS workup
🧠 Practice Questions — Multiple Sclerosis

🔥 Myelitis

LO 1–2 Bimodal 10–19y & 30–39y F ≈ 60% Acute/subacute cord syndrome
Inflammation of the spinal cord — a heterogeneous umbrella spanning demyelinating disease (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD), infectious, postinfectious, systemic autoimmune, paraneoplastic, and idiopathic causes, unified by a transverse-plane interruption of ascending and descending cord pathways.
▶
▶ Transverse Myelitis | Osmosis
Video — "Transverse Myelitis" (Osmosis, YouTube)
1 Natural History

Epidemiology

  • Annual incidence, all-cause myelitis: ~24.6–24.9 per million person-years; idiopathic myelitis specifically: 1.3–8.6 per million person-years
  • Bimodal age distribution — peaks at 10–19y and 30–39y
  • Female predominance (~60%), diminishing after age 60
  • No clear geographic or familial susceptibility pattern for idiopathic forms

Etiology

Autoimmune / Demyelinating

Most common cause overall — MS (~48% of all myelitis patients are eventually diagnosed with MS), NMOSD (AQP4-IgG), MOGAD

Infectious

Direct cord infection: Borrelia (Lyme), HSV-2, VZV, HIV, enterovirus D68, mycoplasma, West Nile virus, CMV

Postinfectious / Post-vaccination

Molecular mimicry — up to 60% of pediatric cases; antecedent infection/vaccination within 6 weeks in ~17% overall

Systemic Autoimmune

SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, sarcoidosis, Sjögren syndrome, Behçet disease

Paraneoplastic

Anti-Hu, anti-CRMP5, anti-amphiphysin antibodies

Idiopathic

15–34% after full workup — though up to 70% of these are reclassified once AQP4-IgG/MOG-IgG testing is applied

Pathophysiology

The pathological hallmark is focal lymphocyte/monocyte infiltration in the spinal cord with variable demyelination, axonal injury, and astroglial/microglial activation.

Molecular mimicry / humoral autoimmunity (AQP4-IgG → astrocytes; MOG-IgG → oligodendrocytes)
→
Perivascular lymphocyte/monocyte infiltration ± complement
→
Demyelination + axonal injury
→
IL-6-mediated injury (correlates with disability)
→
Interruption of ascending/descending tracts
Spinal MRI, T2-weighted — hallmark finding in acute myelitis: T2 hyperintensity within the cord (arrows), often with cord swelling and variable gadolinium enhancement

Prognosis If Untreated

Sobering, though most patients recover some function. Historically, up to 1/3 remained unable to ambulate with 5–10% mortality; modern cohorts report severe disability (mRS ≥3) in 24.7–44.8%. Outcome varies enormously by cause — at 6 months, debilitating symptoms occur in only 2% of MS-associated myelitis vs. 38% of NMOSD vs. 32% of infection-associated myelitis.

Poor-outcome predictors: age ≥50, complete (transverse) myelitis, spinal shock, longitudinally extensive lesions (LETM), elevated CSF PMN count, elevated CSF/serum albumin ratio.

Most recovery occurs in the first 3 months, though improvement can continue for a year or more. Idiopathic/postinfectious forms are usually monophasic; MS and NMOSD are relapsing (27% of idiopathic myelitis relapsed over a 5.4-year median follow-up). High-dose IV corticosteroids are standard empiric first-line therapy (no myelitis-specific RCTs exist), with plasma exchange as rescue for refractory cases.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation

The Motor–Sensory–Autonomic Triad

Symptoms evolve over hours to days (nadir within 1–7 days in ~half, 8–21 days in ~1/3; by diagnostic criteria, progression spans 4 hours to 21 days).

  • Motor (~56%): bilateral, not necessarily symmetric, limb weakness — paraparesis or quadriparesis by level; 50% have complete leg paralysis; hyperreflexia/Babinski (UMN) once past early spinal shock (areflexia + hypotonia)
  • Sensory (96%, most common finding): a well-defined truncal sensory level — the key distinguishing feature from cerebral/peripheral causes; present in 49% as an isolated finding; neuropathic pain and Lhermitte's sign may occur
  • Autonomic (~41%, near-universal to some degree): bladder/bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction
Paroxysmal Tonic Spasms

Involuntary dystonic contractions of limb/trunk muscles lasting 15–60 seconds.

Antecedent Illness

Preceding infection or vaccination within 6 weeks in ~17% of cases; new neck/back pain in ~24%.

Partial vs. Complete

80% present with partial (asymmetric) involvement; complete transverse involvement carries a significantly worse prognosis.

MRI & CSF Characteristics
Lesion pattern by etiology — short-segment lesions (<2 vertebral segments) suggest MS; longitudinally extensive lesions (≥3 segments, LETM) suggest NMOSD/MOGAD. The axial "H-sign" (gray-matter-restricted signal, pink arrowheads) is characteristic of MOG-IgG–associated myelitis.

Lesions are most commonly cervical (65%) and thoracic (53%), with gadolinium enhancement in about 2/3. Brain lesions are found in roughly half of patients. CSF: mononuclear pleocytosis in ~50%, elevated CSF/serum albumin ratio in 30%, increased IgG index in 39%, and oligoclonal bands more often associated with an MS etiology.

Clinical Vignette
📋 Board-Style Vignette
A 22-year-old man presents with three days of progressive bilateral leg weakness and numbness. He describes a clear line across his abdomen below which he cannot feel light touch or pinprick, and he has had new difficulty starting his urine stream. One week before symptom onset, he had a mild upper respiratory illness. On exam his legs are weak and hyporeflexic with decreased tone. MRI of the spine shows a T2-hyperintense lesion spanning the T6–T7 cord segments with patchy enhancement.
What the vignette is testing: a well-defined truncal sensory level plus bladder dysfunction localizes the process to the spinal cord; early hyporeflexia/hypotonia represents spinal shock rather than a peripheral process; the short-segment lesion (under 2 vertebral levels) and antecedent illness point toward a postinfectious or MS-associated etiology rather than NMOSD/MOGAD.

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

  • "clearly demarcated band of altered sensation across the trunk" → sensory level, localizes to the cord
  • "legs are flaccid and areflexic early, then become spastic with a Babinski sign" → spinal shock evolving into UMN signs
  • "lesion spans 3 or more vertebral segments" / "longitudinally extensive" → think NMOSD or MOGAD
  • "short-segment lesion, under 2 vertebral levels" → think MS-associated myelitis
  • "bladder and bowel dysfunction with bilateral leg weakness days after a viral illness or vaccination" → postinfectious transverse myelitis
  • "brief, painful tonic contractions of a limb, several times a day" → paroxysmal tonic spasms
  • "fails to improve after high-dose steroids" → move to plasma exchange as rescue therapy
🧠 Practice Questions — Myelitis

🧸 PANDAS

LO 1–2 Age 5–12y (peak 6–9y) Male predominance reported Post-strep autoimmune
Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal infections — a postinfectious autoimmune disorder in which group A streptococcal (GAS) infection triggers the acute exacerbation of obsessive-compulsive behaviors and tic disorders. Sits on a spectrum with Sydenham chorea.
▶
▶ PANDAS (Year of the Zebra 2025)
Video — "PANDAS" (Year of the Zebra 2025, YouTube)
1 Natural History

Epidemiology

  • First proposed in 1998 (Swedo et al.); precise epidemiological data are still lacking
  • Affects prepubertal children, age 3 through puberty onset — most susceptible 5–12y, mean onset 6–9y
  • GAS pharyngitis (the trigger) is extremely common in this age group; a male predominance has been reported in some cohorts
  • Children with PANS/PANDAS may be at increased risk for subsequent autoimmune disease

Pathogenesis

GAS infection of the pharynx or skin is thought to trigger a cross-reactive antibody response — molecular mimicry — against basal ganglia structures, analogous to the mechanism proposed for Sydenham chorea.

GAS pharyngeal / skin infection
→
Molecular mimicry (cross-reactive antibodies)
→
Anti-striatal cholinergic interneuron Ab + Th17 activation
→
BBB disruption, basal ganglia inflammation
→
Disrupted dopamine signaling
→
Acute-onset OCD / tics

Supporting mechanistic findings: serum IgG from affected children binds specifically to striatal cholinergic interneurons (CINs); animal models show Th17-mediated neurovascular damage and blood-brain barrier disruption; neuroimaging shows acute basal ganglia swelling with microglial activation; CaM kinase II activation disrupts basal ganglia dopamine release.

An Unsettled Diagnosis

The PANDAS hypothesis remains controversial. A large Danish nationwide cohort (N = 1,067,743 children) found streptococcal throat infection increased risk of OCD (IRR 1.51) and tic disorders (IRR 1.35) — but nonstreptococcal throat infections also carried elevated risk, questioning the specificity of the GAS association. Some prospective studies with intensive clinical observation did not find that strep infections consistently preceded neuropsychiatric worsening.

Prognosis If Untreated

Follows a relapsing-remitting pattern of flares between quiescent periods. In one prospective study (33 children, mean 3.3y follow-up): 88% were free of clinically significant OCD at follow-up, but 72% had experienced ≥1 exacerbation (median 1, range 1–12) along the way — outcomes better overall than childhood-onset OCD, supporting a "subacute illness" model similar to Sydenham chorea, though some children develop a chronic course.

A large Italian cohort (N = 371) on long-term antibiotic prophylaxis found 75% improved within 3–5 months, though 45% of the total cohort had infection-related relapses long-term. Early diagnosis appears important to reduce the risk of progression toward chronic neurologic sequelae. Without treatment, the concern is cumulative neuropsychiatric morbidity from repeated GAS-triggered flares, with possible evolution toward a chronic, less episodic course.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation

The Hallmark: "Overnight" Onset

PANDAS is defined by the dramatic, abrupt onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms following GAS infection — distinguishing it from the typically gradual onset of childhood OCD or Tourette syndrome. Onset occurs within 3 years of GAS exposure, with an acute, episodic ("sawtooth") course and slow resolution between flares.

Cardinal symptoms: obsessive-compulsive disorder (often severe — contamination fears, symmetry obsessions, ritualistic behaviors appearing abruptly) and tic disorders (motor and/or vocal, acute onset).

Emotional / Behavioral
  • Severe separation anxiety
  • Emotional lability, irritability, rage
  • Developmental regression ("baby talk," clinginess)
Academic / Motor
  • Acute decline in handwriting (dysgraphia)
  • School performance decline
  • Choreiform movements, motor hyperactivity, fine-motor decline
Somatic
  • Sleep disturbance, nightmares
  • New-onset enuresis, urinary frequency
  • Eating restriction (can mimic anorexia); sensory amplification to light/sound/texture

Key Discriminators

The onset of choreiform movements or other motoric hyperactivity is more suggestive of Sydenham chorea than PANDAS. A systematic review notes that acute OCD onset combined with separation anxiety, irritability, emotional lability, or dysgraphia should specifically prompt consideration of a postinfectious etiology. DSM-5-TR recognizes PANDAS as a postinfectious autoimmune disorder with sudden OCD/tics plus acute neuropsychiatric symptoms — in the absence of chorea, carditis, or arthritis (features that instead point toward acute rheumatic fever/Sydenham chorea).

Clinical Vignette
📋 Board-Style Vignette
A 7-year-old boy is brought in by his parents because "overnight" he became consumed with fear of germs, began washing his hands until they bled, and now refuses to sleep alone. His teacher also reports his handwriting has become illegible over the past week and his grades have dropped sharply. Two weeks ago he was treated for streptococcal pharyngitis confirmed by a rapid strep test. On exam he has occasional brief, jerky movements of his fingers but no true chorea, and no rash, joint swelling, or cardiac murmur.
What the vignette is testing: the abrupt, "overnight" onset of severe OCD after a documented GAS infection is the hallmark of PANDAS; the dysgraphia, separation anxiety, and academic decline are supporting features; the absence of true chorea, carditis, and arthritis argues against acute rheumatic fever/Sydenham chorea.

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

  • "literally overnight" / "abrupt onset" of OCD or tics → the single most tested PANDAS buzz phrase
  • "sore throat" or "scarlet fever" one to six weeks prior → antecedent GAS trigger
  • "sudden clinginess," "won't sleep alone," "baby talk" → developmental regression / separation anxiety
  • "handwriting has gotten worse," "grades dropped suddenly" → dysgraphia and academic decline
  • "new bedwetting" in a previously toilet-trained child → new-onset enuresis
  • "choreiform movements" or "writhing movements of the hands" → think Sydenham chorea instead, especially with carditis or arthritis
  • "positive ASO or anti-DNase B titer" → supportive, but not required, lab evidence of recent GAS infection
